subject: rent comps and how to read them
preheader: a median or automated estimate is not a property-specific lease comp.
headline: Rent evidence needs consistent property and location filters.
body: Automated rent products can use different records, geographic boundaries, dates, property filters, and statistical methods. A disagreement needs investigation; it is not proof that one source is correct.

For a hypothetical range of $1,400 to $2,800 around a $2,000 median, check whether bedroom count, size, condition, concessions, utilities, lease date, and neighborhood boundaries explain the spread. The numbers are illustrative, not a current market claim.

Review current comparable listings and, where available, executed leases with similar location, beds, baths, size, condition, amenities, and included utilities. Asking rent is not collected rent, so record the source and date for each comp.
When evidence supports more than one rent case, model the range as separate scenarios rather than selecting a universal low or median rule. Verify the chosen input before anyone relies on the result.

When the comp lookup is available under your plan, TrueCap can show RentCast sale and rent comps from the address. The separate HUD area-rent value is a screening benchmark, not another property-specific comp source. Compare both with current local evidence before relying on a rent assumption.
